flashcard_questions.a: A poem where one character speaks to a silent listener, revealing their own personality.

flashcard_questions.q: Which real duke is the speaker of the poem based on?
Who was the Duke’s first wife, dead at sixteen?
Why has the emissary come to see the Duke?
flashcard_questions.a: To arrange the Duke’s next marriage for the Count of Tyrol.

flashcard_questions.q: What is chilling about the phrase ‘as if she were alive’?
flashcard_questions.a: It hints that she is dead, perhaps killed by his commands.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the word ‘last’ imply about the Duchess?
flashcard_questions.a: She is one in a series, an item in his collection.

flashcard_questions.q: Which gift does the Duke resent the Duchess treating as ordinary?
Which line implies the Duke had the Duchess killed?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘I gave commands; then all smiles stopped together.’

flashcard_questions.q: What does the euphemism ‘all smiles stopped together’ imply?
flashcard_questions.a: That she was killed, since only death stops someone smiling for ever.

flashcard_questions.q: Which statue does the Duke point out as the two men leave?
What does that bronze statue symbolise about the Duke?
flashcard_questions.a: His wish to dominate, as the god dominates the sea-horse.

flashcard_questions.q: Which object shows the Duke now controls who sees the Duchess?
Which rhyme scheme gives the poem its sense of order and control?
Which technique works against that regularity, spilling speech over line ends?
Why does Browning keep the emissary silent throughout?
flashcard_questions.a: It mirrors the power imbalance — the Duke dominates every voice.

notes: 15 cards: 4 quotation-to-effect (‘as if she were alive’, ‘last’, the euphemism, the statue), 3 quotation-recall fronts (the commands line, the nine-hundred-years-old name, the curtain), 4 structure-and-form cards (rhyming couplets, enjambment, the silent listener, the monologue definition), 3 context facts (Alfonso II, Lucrezia, the emissary’s errand), 1 symbol card (Neptune). The existing poet and poem-title cards were not repeated. ‘Caesurae’, ‘symbol’ and ‘iambic pentameter’ dropped as glossary restatements. All quotations verbatim from the lesson content.
